summary: This unit teaches you to use complex workplace communication strategies as a manager in a Jamaican public body or business. You will learn to analyse audiences and stakeholders, plan a communication strategy and key messages, choose channels and adapt to different needs, handle difficult conversations and conflict, facilitate meetings and consultations, represent your unit, write briefing notes and evaluate whether your communication worked.

blocks.p: Everyday communication is giving and receiving simple information. **Complex communication** is needed when the message is difficult or sensitive, the audiences are many and different, people disagree or are upset, or the decision is contentious: closing an office, changing a fee, relocating vendors, restructuring jobs. In these cases, a manager needs a **deliberate strategy**, not just an announcement.

This unit is for Level 5 supervisors and managers in ministries, agencies, municipal corporations, schools and businesses. It covers the thinking (who needs to know what, when and how), the skills (listening, explaining, facilitating, negotiating) and the checking (did the message reach and work?).

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in your work
rows: Find out each group's needs, concerns, knowledge and influence, and map them on a power-interest grid.
Set objectives, key messages, channels, sequence, spokespeople and a timetable.
Use plain language and suit literacy, disability, culture, age, distance and technology.
Listen actively, stay calm, de-escalate, give bad news with care and keep to safety procedures.
Hear each party, find the real needs and look for options that work for both.
Set purpose, agenda and ground rules; manage dominant and silent members; record outcomes.
Represent the unit and write for leaders
Prepare for inter-agency meetings, know your authority and write briefing notes.
Check understanding, collect feedback and review channels and messages.

ul: A multiple-choice theory paper with scenario questions on audiences, channels, difficult conversations, conflict, facilitation and evaluation.
A written paper with short answers (power-interest grid, paraphrasing, consensus, ground rules, I statements, briefing note, communication audit) and longer plans.
Group practicals: planning a communication strategy for a contentious decision, and facilitating a consultation and a difficult conversation in role-play.

blocks.note: Whenever a scenario is complex, start by asking: who are the audiences, what does each need, and what is the right order of communication?
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A contentious decision, such as closing a rural police station or moving a market, affects many people in different ways. Without a plan, rumours spread, different people hear different things, staff learn from the media and trust is lost. A strategy makes sure that the right people hear the right message, from the right person, at the right time. **Poor communication** can cause anger, loss of trust, resistance, wasted time and damage to the body's reputation.
Start by analysing each audience: **what they need, what worries them, what they already know, and how they prefer to receive information.**

head: Question
Why it matters
rows: Shows who must be told, and what is at stake for them
What do they already know or believe?
Avoids repeating, correcting or contradicting what they think
Lets you address real worries, not only your own agenda
What do they need to do or decide?
How do they prefer to get information?

blocks.p: A **power-interest grid** sorts stakeholders by how much power they have over the decision or its success, and how interested they are.

head: Power
Low interest
High interest
rows: **Manage closely (involve):** consult often, involve in decisions

blocks.p: For example, a senior ministry committee with high power and high interest should be **involved closely and consulted often**. A citizens' association that is very interested but has little formal power should be **kept well informed, and its views listened to**. Their goodwill can make or break a project.

flow: Set the objective: what must people know, feel or do?
Analyse the audiences and map the stakeholders
Write three to five key messages in plain language
Choose the channels and spokespeople for each audience
Decide the order and timing: who hears first, and when
Prepare for questions and for the hardest conversations
Brief all front-line staff so that everyone gives the same answers
Deliver, listen and adjust
Evaluate and report

ul: Keep to **three to five** key messages: what is happening, why, what it means for you, what you can do and where to get help.
Use short sentences and everyday words.
Say what is known, what is not yet known and when people will hear more.
Repeat the same core messages in every channel.
Test them on someone outside the project.

blocks.p: People who are most affected, especially staff, should normally hear first, directly and in person, before the media or the public. If the staff of a regional office that is to close learn from the news, trust is destroyed. Plan so that staff hear the news from their own managers before public announcements. Likewise, brief front-line staff so that **everyone gives the same answers** to the public.

blocks.note: Do not make promises you cannot keep. If no decision has been made, say what is known, what is not known and when people will hear. A promise broken later does more harm than an honest "not yet decided".
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Choose timing carefully. A two-week public consultation held in the Christmas season, or at the height of the hurricane season, will give few people time to respond well. Allow enough time and give notice through channels people use.

sections.title: Choosing channels and adapting the message

head: Channel
Best for
Weakness
rows: Complex, contentious or sensitive issues; people can ask questions and you see reactions
Personal impact, such as a changed job
Easy to ignore or misread; one way
Little chance to ask questions; message can be distorted
Cameras off, poor connection, fewer reactions seen

blocks.p: For a complex, contentious message, use a combination: a **meeting first, then one-to-one talks and a written summary.** Face-to-face is usually better than email for contentious issues because people can ask questions and you can see reactions.

ul: One idea per sentence. Put the most important point first.
Choose everyday words. Explain unavoidable technical terms.
Use the active voice: "You must apply by 1 May" rather than "Applications are to be submitted by applicants."
Give dates, amounts and steps exactly.
Avoid long chains of technical details; give the key points first and offer more.

head: Hard to understand
Plain version
rows: "Eligibility is contingent upon continuous residency for a period of not less than twelve months."
"From 1 May, you must have lived here for a year to qualify."
"Remittances must be effected prior to the expiration of the fiscal quarter."
"Pay before the end of the quarter."

head: Audience
What to do
rows: Talk it through, show the steps with pictures or demonstration, check understanding by asking them to explain it back, avoid forms in dense text
Large print, screen-reader files, audio, readers
A qualified sign language interpreter; written notes; face the person and speak clearly
Check understanding, avoid slang and idioms, allow time, respect customs
Clear print, face-to-face or phone, patience, and offline options
Radio, community meetings, noticeboards, phone, as well as online
Same facts, with examples and channels to suit each: for example business owners and elderly homeowners hearing about a new tax rule

blocks.p: The **same facts** must be told to every group; what changes is the example, the language and the channel.

ul: Send the agenda and papers in advance.
At the start, agree how people will take part: hands, chat, names.
Call people by name; use polls and the chat to draw people in.
Ask people to turn cameras on if they can and if it is appropriate.
Keep to time and summarise decisions at the end.

blocks.note: Not everyone in rural districts has reliable internet. Offer a phone line or an in-person option for public sessions, and make a recording or a summary available after.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Technical content for a public audience

blocks.p: When a technical report, such as one on water quality, must be shared with a citizens' association, write a **plain-language summary** and offer a briefing. Ask the technical experts to check your summary for accuracy. A summary that changes the meaning is worse than none.

sections.title: Difficult conversations, bad news and de-escalation

blocks.p: **Active listening** means giving full attention and showing you understand. Its skills include:

head: Skill
What it looks like
rows: Face the person, put aside your phone, give eye contact as appropriate
Short prompts such as "Go on" or "I see"
"Can you tell me what happened, from the start?"
Restating what you heard in your own words: "So the main problem is that you were sent away twice?"
Pulling the main points together and checking them
"I can see this has been frustrating."
Allow pauses so that the person can continue

blocks.p: **Empathy** is the ability to understand and share how another person feels. It does not mean agreeing; it means showing that you have heard.
**De-escalation** means reducing the tension in a heated exchange. Staying calm, listening and acknowledging the concern are the main tools.

flow: Stay calm: lower your voice, slow down, keep open body language
Let the person speak without interrupting
Acknowledge feelings and the problem ("I understand why you are upset")
Paraphrase to show you understood
Focus on what can be done, and explain the next step clearly
Offer a time and person for follow-up
If the person becomes threatening, follow the safety procedure and get help

blocks.note: Your safety comes first. If a person becomes threatening, do not argue or try to restrain him. Follow the office's safety procedure, call for help or security, and report afterwards.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: When you must tell a person that an application has been refused or that a service will end, **explain the reasons clearly and the next steps**.

flow: Prepare the facts and choose a private place
Say early, simply and kindly what the decision is
Give the reasons in plain language
Allow time for reaction without hurrying
Explain what the person can do next: appeal, reapply, alternative help
Record what was said and follow up

blocks.p: With people who are distressed, such as a family receiving bad news, speak gently, give the key facts and allow time. Do not overload them with detail; offer to repeat or send a written summary.

**I statements** express a view without blaming the other person. "I am concerned when reports arrive late, because it delays the whole team" is better than "You are always late." They keep the focus on the issue and make it easier for the other person to listen.

If a resident shares private information about a neighbour during a consultation, leave it out of public notes and follow policy. Remind everyone that comments should be about the issue, not about individuals.
After a difficult consultation or conversation, reflect on feedback and plan what to change. Ask a colleague what went well and what to do differently. Skills grow when you review them.

ul: Different interests or goals (two units need the same resource)
Unclear roles or rules
Poor communication or rumours
Personality and style differences
Pressure, stress or unfairness

blocks.p: Conflict is not always bad: it shows that people care and can lead to better solutions if managed well. Left alone, it grows, staff take sides and work suffers.

A **position** is what a person says they want ("I must have the room on Monday"). An **interest** is why they want it ("I need privacy for interviews"). Two positions may clash while the real interests can both be met. Always look for the **underlying needs** and for options that meet both real needs.

flow: Meet each person separately and listen without taking sides
Find the facts and the real needs behind each position
Bring the parties together with agreed ground rules
Let each state their view, uninterrupted, then paraphrase
Identify the shared goal and the points of agreement
Generate options together; avoid judging at first
Choose the option that best meets both sets of needs
Agree actions, dates and a follow-up
Check later that the agreement is working

head: Role
What the person does
rows: Hears both sides, sets fair rules and may decide if the parties cannot agree
A neutral person who helps both parties reach their own agreement without deciding for them
Guides a discussion towards its aims, without taking sides

ul: Prepare: know your needs, your limits and what you can offer.
Focus on interests, not positions.
Look for a **win-win** outcome where both gain something.
Be firm on the problem, gentle with the people.
Use objective standards (rules, data, precedent) to judge the options.
Put the final agreement in writing.

blocks.note: If two senior officers disagree openly, meet each privately first to hear their concerns. Settling it in front of the team would deepen the split.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **facilitator** guides a group towards its aims without taking sides. The facilitator does not push a view; she makes sure the process is fair, everyone can speak and the group reaches an outcome.

ul: Clarify the purpose and the decisions needed
Invite the right people, in good time, with the agenda and papers
Choose a suitable venue and time, with access for all
Plan the sequence and times
Decide how outcomes will be recorded and shared

blocks.p: At the start of a workshop, **agree the purpose, agenda and ground rules**. **Ground rules** are the agreed rules for behaviour, for example: one person speaks at a time, respect other views, phones on silent, keep to time and confidentiality of personal comments.

head: Situation
What the facilitator does
rows: Thank him, and invite the others' views in turn
Ask them directly and gently; use small groups or written ideas
An important point outside the agenda
Note it on a "parking lot" list for later follow-up
Remind people of the ground rules; pause; return to the question
Acknowledge, offer a break if needed and continue
Return to the agenda and summarise what has been agreed

head: Tool
How it works
rows: People put forward as many ideas as possible without judging them; then group and discuss
Members write ideas silently, share them in turn, then rank them
Score options against agreed criteria, such as cost, speed and fairness
A decision that all members can accept, even if it is not everyone's first choice
A quick decision where there is a clear choice; some may feel unheard

blocks.p: When a working group cannot agree on one option, the fairest method is usually to **rank the options against agreed criteria**.

ul: Sum up agreements, actions and next steps.
Confirm who does what and by when.
Thank participants.
Write up the outcomes soon after the meeting and share them, so that all can check that their views were recorded fairly.
A consultation paper should state clearly **what is still open to change**, so people know where their views can count.
Give enough time, notice and a range of ways to respond (meetings, written, phone).
Report back: what you heard, what you will do and why.
When a director receives strong criticism at a town hall meeting, she should thank people, ask questions and say what happens next. Do not become defensive.

sections.title: Representing your unit and writing for leaders

flow: Find out the purpose, agenda and who will attend
Agree the unit's position and limits with your manager
Collect facts and figures; prepare questions
At the meeting, speak for the unit and listen carefully
Do not commit beyond your authority: say you will take the matter back and reply by an agreed date
Record decisions and actions
Report back to your manager and follow up on actions

blocks.p: If another agency asks you to lend staff and you have no authority to agree, say that you will take it back and reply by an agreed date. Agree contacts, channels and a joint plan when several agencies work together, such as a joint service centre.

A **briefing note** is a short document that sets out an issue, the options and a recommendation for a senior decision-maker. A good structure is: **purpose, key facts, options and a recommendation**. Keep it short, accurate and neutral where facts are concerned.

ul: Put the purpose and the decision needed first.
Give the key facts, with figures checked twice.
Present realistic options with pros and cons.
Make a clear recommendation that follows from the analysis.
Use plain language, define abbreviations and keep it to one or two pages.

blocks.h: From briefing note to public leaflet

blocks.p: The same content may be used for a leaflet for the public, but written differently: shorter, in plain language, with the actions people must take and where to get help. Remove internal detail and confidential material.

To ask for money for a new system, present the **evidence, costs, benefits and options**. Show the problem with data, show what the proposed solution would do and what it costs, and show what happens if nothing is done.
A speaker talks at about 130 words a minute. To prepare a talk of a given length, multiply: a 7-minute talk is about 7 × 130 = 910 words. Add time for pauses and questions.

head: Method
What it shows
rows: Whether people know the message and what they have done, for example a survey on dengue prevention knowledge and practice
How many came or replied; for example 224 of 320 invited (70%)
Whether behaviour has changed, such as the number of breeding sites removed
Where staff first heard of changes

blocks.p: Measure results against the objective: not only whether messages were sent, but whether they were understood and acted on.

A **communication audit** is a review of how well an organisation communicates, covering its channels, messages and the views of staff and users. If a staff survey shows that many officers learn about changes from the media first, management should **review its internal channels and their timing**.

ul: Fix channels that fail: for example, brief staff first.
Keep what works.
Share lessons with colleagues.
Keep a short record of what you did and what you would change.
explain why a deliberate communication strategy is needed for complex or contentious messages.
analyse an audience and map stakeholders on a power-interest grid.
plan objectives, key messages, channels, sequence and spokespeople.
explain why affected staff should usually hear first, and why front-line staff need the same answers.
choose the best channel for a message and combine channels.
write in plain language and adapt for literacy, disability, culture, age and distance.
listen actively, paraphrase and show empathy.
de-escalate a heated exchange and follow safety procedures.
give bad news with clear reasons and next steps.
use I statements and avoid blame.
tell positions from interests and resolve conflict with win-win options.
facilitate a meeting: agree purpose, agenda and ground rules; manage dominant and quiet members; use a parking lot, brainstorming, nominal group technique, ranking and consensus.
run a consultation that says what is open to change and reports back.
represent my unit within my authority and report back.
write a briefing note and adapt it for the public.
evaluate communication with surveys, feedback and a communication audit.

terms: Complex communication
Communication that is difficult or sensitive, involves many audiences or has people who disagree or are upset.
Stakeholder
A person or group affected by a decision or able to influence it.
Power-interest grid
A grid that sorts stakeholders by how much power they have and how interested they are.
Key messages
The three to five main points that every channel and speaker repeats.
Plain language
Writing or speech that the intended reader can understand the first time.
Active listening
Giving full attention and checking understanding.
Paraphrasing
Restating what a speaker said in your own words to check understanding.
Empathy
Understanding and sharing how another person feels.
De-escalation
Reducing tension in a heated exchange.
I statement
A statement that expresses a view without blaming, such as "I am concerned when reports arrive late".
Position
What a person says they want.
Interest
The reason behind what a person wants.
Mediator
A neutral person who helps two parties reach their own agreement.
Facilitator
A person who guides a group towards its aims without taking sides.
Ground rules
Agreed rules for behaviour, set at the start of a meeting or workshop.
Brainstorming
Putting forward as many ideas as possible without judging them.
Nominal group technique
Writing ideas silently, sharing them in turn, then ranking them.
Consensus
A decision every member can accept, even if it is not everyone's first choice.
Briefing note
A short document setting out an issue, the options and a recommendation for a senior decision-maker.
Communication audit
A review of an organisation's channels, messages and the views of staff and users.

c1.title: Paid parking in Ocho Rios
c1.text: A municipal corporation in St Ann plans to introduce paid parking in the Ocho Rios town centre in three months. Taxi operators, shop owners, vendors, residents, the police and the council's finance committee will all be affected. The shop owners and finance committee have high power. The residents' association is very interested but has little formal power. The communications officer, Ms Charmaine Walker, is drafting the plan. Front-line parking attendants will answer questions from the public.

c2.title: A dispute over late supplier payments
c2.text: In a ministry in Kingston, the procurement unit and the finance unit blame each other for late payments to suppliers. The two heads, Mr Aubrey Lyn and Mrs Donna Reid, have stopped speaking. Procurement says it needs finance to confirm funds on the same day; finance says it needs complete files before it can confirm funds. The Director, Mr Paul Henry, decides to step in as their manager.

c3.title: A drainage consultation in Hanover
c3.text: A parish office in Hanover holds a community meeting about a drainage project that will pass through several farms. Sixty residents attend. A farmer, Mr Cecil Brown, speaks at length and loudly, while several older women say nothing. Some residents raise a problem with a broken bridge, which is not part of the project. Some have low literacy. The facilitator is Ms Yvonne Clarke.

c4.title: An upset customer at a registry counter
c4.text: At a registry counter in Spanish Town, Mr Winston Thomas, a customer, becomes loud because his application for a certificate has been delayed twice and he has taken time off work. A clerk, Ms Shanice Morris, must respond. Later, a second customer, Mrs Hortense Gray, must be told that her application is refused because a document is missing.

c5.title: Representing the unit on a drought committee
c5.text: Mrs Latoya Francis represents a ministry's rural development unit on an inter-agency drought response committee. The first meeting is tomorrow. Another agency will ask her unit to lend two vehicles for three weeks, but Mrs Francis has no authority to agree to this. She has been asked to give a 7-minute report at the meeting. After the meeting, she must prepare a note for the Permanent Secretary and a leaflet for farmers.

questions.q: The council's finance committee has high power over the scheme but little day-to-day interest in it. How should Ms Walker treat it?
o: Keep it satisfied with short updates at key decision points
Involve it in every detail of the plan and consult it every week
Monitor it and send it only the general public notices that issue
Leave it out of the process until after the scheme is announced
questions.why: A group with high power but low interest should be kept satisfied: brief and not overloaded, but never surprised, since it can stop the scheme.

questions.q: The corporation has three months. Who should hear about the scheme first, and how?
o: Residents, through a notice placed in the daily newspaper by the council
Shop owners, vendors and taxi operators, in direct meetings
Everyone at the same time, through radio and social media posts
The media, through a press release explaining why the scheme is needed
questions.why: People most affected should hear directly and early, before general announcements, so that they do not learn about it second-hand.

questions.q: Parking attendants will answer public questions. What is the best preparation?
o: Tell them to refer every question they receive to the council's office
Give them a leaflet to hand out to drivers and no other instructions
Brief them on the key messages so that all give the same answers
Let them answer as they see fit, since they know the town and drivers
questions.why: If different officers give different answers, trust is lost. Front-line staff need agreed key messages and a place to refer difficult questions.

questions.q: After the launch, how can the corporation best check whether its messages were understood?
o: Count the number of notices that were printed and posted
Ask the attendants how many questions they were asked
Wait for complaints, since these will show any confusion
Survey drivers and traders on what they know and do
questions.why: Evaluation looks at understanding and action, not only at activity. A short survey of those affected shows what was understood.

questions.q: Mr Henry wants to resolve the dispute. What should he do first?
o: Meet each head privately to hear their concerns
Call a joint meeting and ask each head to apologise to the other
Send a circular to both units telling them to cooperate fully
Wait for the two heads to resolve the dispute by themselves
questions.why: Meeting each privately lets each speak freely and shows fairness. The joint meeting comes later, with ground rules.

questions.q: Procurement says 'Finance must confirm funds the same day.' Finance says 'We need complete files first.' How should Mr Henry see these statements?
o: As interests that cannot be changed by any discussion between them
As positions, with interests behind them that he should discover
As proof that the finance unit is the cause of all the delays
As proof that procurement files are never complete when sent
questions.why: A position is what each says it wants; interests are why. Looking at why, such as a need for speed and a need for accuracy, opens options that meet both.

questions.q: Which option is most likely to meet the real needs of both units?
o: Instruct finance to confirm funds on the same day for every file
Instruct procurement to send all of its files only on Fridays
A joint checklist for files, with a same-day funds check
Transfer the funds confirmation task to the procurement unit
questions.why: The joint checklist addresses finance's need for complete files and procurement's need for speed. It is a win-win solution that both can accept.

questions.q: Mrs Reid says to Mr Lyn, 'You are always sending me rubbish files.' Which I statement says it better?
o: I would like you to try much harder with the files from now on
I think your unit is careless in preparing the files for payment
I do not want to see another incomplete file from any of your staff
I am worried when files lack documents, as it delays payment
questions.why: An I statement describes the speaker's concern and its effect without blaming the other person, so the other party can listen.

questions.q: Mr Brown dominates the meeting. What should Ms Clarke do?
o: Thank him for his views and invite others to speak in turn
Ask him to leave the meeting until the others have finished speaking
Allow him to continue at length, since he is the most affected farmer
Tell him that the other residents are tired of hearing him talk
questions.why: Politely managing a dominant speaker keeps the meeting fair. Inviting others in turn makes space for the quiet ones without shaming anyone.

questions.q: Residents raise the broken bridge, which is outside the project. What should Ms Clarke do?
o: Discuss it fully now, since it matters a great deal to the residents
Note it on a list for later follow-up and return to the agenda
Tell them firmly that the bridge is not a matter for this meeting
Ask the project manager to promise that the bridge will be repaired
questions.why: A 'parking lot' list records the issue so that it is not ignored, and keeps the meeting on its purpose. Follow up afterwards and tell residents the outcome.

questions.q: Some residents have low literacy. How should the project be explained?
o: Hand out a detailed written summary for people to read at home
Show a long slide presentation that includes the technical drawings
Talk through the steps, use a map and check understanding
Leave the explanation to a neighbour who can read the documents well
questions.why: People with low literacy learn best from spoken explanation and visuals, with a check that they have understood.

questions.q: Ms Clarke wants every resident to contribute ideas on where to place access points, without anyone dominating or judging. Which technique suits this best?
o: An open vote by a show of hands on the first idea that is suggested
A long open discussion led by the most senior person who is present
A written petition that residents sign before the meeting begins
The nominal group technique: write silently, share, then rank
questions.why: Silent writing gives everyone a voice, sharing in turn stops domination and ranking gives a fair result.

questions.q: Mr Thomas is loud and angry. Which response from Ms Morris is best?
o: 'You have been delayed twice and lost work time. Let me see what I can do.'
'Sir, please lower your voice or I will not be able to help you today.'
'This is not my fault, so there is no need to shout at me like this.'
'Everyone has to wait their turn, and you are no different from the others.'
questions.why: Paraphrasing and acknowledging his problem shows she has heard him, and moves the talk towards action.

questions.q: Mr Thomas starts to threaten Ms Morris. What should she do?
o: Match his tone so that he understands that she is serious
Follow the safety procedure and call for help
Leave the counter and say nothing
Give him what he wants so that he calms down
questions.why: A threat changes the situation. Personal safety comes first: follow the office procedure, get help and report it.

questions.q: Mrs Gray's application is refused because a document is missing. What is the best way to tell her?
o: Tell her it is refused and ask her to read the notice on the wall
Give the reason in writing only and call the next customer forward
Explain what is missing and how to resubmit, with time for questions
Tell her to contact the unit head to discuss the matter further
questions.why: Bad news should include clear reasons and next steps, delivered with respect. Leaving her without a way forward would increase her frustration.

questions.q: The other agency asks for two vehicles for three weeks. What should Mrs Francis say?
o: She will lend the vehicles if her unit's manager is willing
She cannot help, because the unit needs them
She will lend them for the first week and review later
She will take it back and reply by an agreed date
questions.why: She cannot commit beyond her authority. Taking it back and replying by a firm date is honest and keeps the relationship.

questions.q: What should Mrs Francis do before the first meeting?
o: Agree the unit's position and limits with her manager
Prepare to agree to whatever the committee suggests on the day
Decide the unit's position on her own, to avoid any delay
Wait to hear the other agencies' views first at the meeting
questions.why: Representing a unit requires an agreed position and clear limits on what she can promise, so that she can speak with confidence.

questions.q: About how many words should a 7-minute report contain if she speaks at 130 words a minute?
o: About 650
About 910
About 1,300
About 1,560
questions.why: 7 × 130 = 910 words. Allow a little less if she plans for pauses and questions.

questions.q: How should the leaflet for farmers differ from the note for the Permanent Secretary?
o: The same text, with the Permanent Secretary's name taken off the top
Longer, with the full background, so that farmers see all the detail
Shorter and plainer, with actions for farmers and where to get help
Written in technical terms, so that it is accurate and exact in its meaning
questions.why: The same content serves different readers if adapted: farmers need plain words, the steps to take and who to contact, without internal or confidential detail.

questions.q: A director sends an email to 300 staff announcing a change in job duties. Within a day, staff are giving each other conflicting versions of what it means. What should she do next?
o: Send a second, longer email repeating the first in more detail
Ask supervisors to tell staff that the email is clear
Wait a week to see whether the rumours fade by themselves
Hold unit meetings with a short question-and-answer sheet
questions.why: An email is one-way and easy to misread. For a sensitive change, follow it with face-to-face briefings where people can ask questions, and a short written summary.
